claim: Basigin is an essential host receptor for invasion of Plasmodium falciparum into human erythrocytes, interacting with parasite surface protein PfRH5.
source: Basigin is an essential host receptor for invasion of Plasmodium falciparum into human erythrocytes, interacting with parasite surface protein PfRH5.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Crosnier et al., 2011) in the introduction.

claim: PfRH5 is a leading blood-stage malaria vaccine candidate and a target of growth-inhibitory antibodies.
source: PfRH5 is a leading blood-stage malaria vaccine candidate and a target of growth-inhibitory antibodies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations in the introduction (Payne et al., 2017; Minassian et al., 2021).

claim: Erythrocyte basigin is exclusively found in one of two macromolecular complexes, bound either to plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase 1/4 (PMCA1/4) or to monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1).
source: Here, we show that erythrocyte basigin is exclusively found in one of two macromolecular complexes, bound either to plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase 1/4 (PMCA1/4) or to monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: PfRH5 binds to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 complexes with a higher affinity than to isolated basigin ectodomain.
source: PfRH5 binds to each of these complexes with a higher affinity than to isolated basigin ectodomain, making it likely that these are the physiological targets of PfRH5.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PMCA-mediated Ca2+ export is not affected by PfRH5.
source: PMCA-mediated Ca2+ export is not affected by PfRH5, making it unlikely that this is the mechanism underlying changes in calcium flux at the interface between an erythrocyte and the invading parasite.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2e and 2f.

claim: Growth-inhibitory antibodies R5.016 and 9AD4 do not reduce the binding of PfRH5 to monomeric basigin.
source: While these antibodies do not reduce the binding of PfRH5 to monomeric basigin, they do reduce its binding to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data in Figure 4.

claim: Growth-inhibitory antibodies R5.016 and 9AD4 reduce PfRH5 binding to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 complexes.
source: While these antibodies do not reduce the binding of PfRH5 to monomeric basigin, they do reduce its binding to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data in Figure 4.

claim: The most effective PfRH5-targeting antibodies inhibit growth by sterically blocking the essential interaction of PfRH5 with basigin in its physiological context.
source: This indicates that the most effective PfRH5-targeting antibodies inhibit growth by sterically blocking the essential interaction of PfRH5 with basigin in its physiological context.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by structural modeling and SPR data in Figure 4.

claim: Malaria is still one of the most deadly parasitic diseases to affect humans, with Plasmodium falciparum as the causative agent of the most severe cases.
source: Malaria is still one of the most deadly parasitic diseases to affect humans, with Plasmodium falciparum as the causative agent of the most severe cases (Sato, 2021).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation to Sato, 2021.

claim: The binding of merozoite P. falciparum reticulocyte homologue 5 (PfRH5) to erythrocyte basigin is essential for invasion by all tested P. falciparum strains.
source: While many of these interactions are redundant, the binding of merozoite P. falciparum reticulocyte homologue 5 (PfRH5) to erythrocyte basigin is essential for invasion by all tested P. falciparum strains (Crosnier et al., 2011), making PfRH5 one of the most promising blood-stage malaria vaccine candidates.
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Crosnier et al., 2011.

claim: PfRH5 is part of the five-component PfPCRCR complex, containing PfRH5, PfCyRPA, PfRIPR, PfPTRAMP, and PfCSS.
source: PfRH5 is part of the five-component PfPCRCR complex, containing PfRH5, PfCyRPA, PfRIPR, PfPTRAMP, and PfCSS, and each component is essential for invasion and is a target of growth-inhibitory antibodies or nanobodies (Farrell et al., 2023; Reddy et al., 2015; Scally et al., 2022; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each component of the PfPCRCR complex is essential for invasion and is a target of growth-inhibitory antibodies or nanobodies.
source: PfRH5 is part of the five-component PfPCRCR complex, containing PfRH5, PfCyRPA, PfRIPR, PfPTRAMP, and PfCSS, and each component is essential for invasion and is a target of growth-inhibitory antibodies or nanobodies (Farrell et al., 2023; Reddy et al., 2015; Scally et al., 2022; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Vaccination of human volunteers with PfRH5 elicits strain-transcending anti-malarial antibodies.
source: Vaccination of human volunteers with PfRH5 elicits strain-transcending anti-malarial antibodies (Payne et al., 2017) and, in a human challenge model, reduces the rate of parasite growth (Minassian et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Payne et al., 2017.

claim: In a human challenge model, PfRH5 vaccination reduces the rate of parasite growth.
source: Vaccination of human volunteers with PfRH5 elicits strain-transcending anti-malarial antibodies (Payne et al., 2017) and, in a human challenge model, reduces the rate of parasite growth (Minassian et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Minassian et al., 2021.

claim: Basigin binds towards one of the tips of the 'kite-like' structure of PfRH5.
source: Structural studies of PfRH5 have revealed that basigin binds towards one of the tips of the 'kite-like' structure of PfRH5 (Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Wright et al., 2014.

claim: Structures of PfRH5 in complex with Fab fragments of monoclonal antibodies have identified a number of important epitopes across PfRH5, including those for human and mouse growth-inhibitory antibodies (R5.004, R5.016, 9AD4, and QA1).
source: Structures of PfRH5 in complex with Fab fragments of monoclonal antibodies have identified a number of important epitopes across PfRH5, including those for human and mouse growth-inhibitory antibodies (R5.004, R5.016, 9AD4, and QA1) (Alanine et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2014), as well as the epitope for an antibody which potentiates the effects of growth-inhibitory antibodies (R5.011) (Alanine et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Alanine et al., 2019 and Wright et al., 2014.

claim: The most effective growth-inhibitory antibodies, 9AD4 and R5.016, are not able to block basigin binding.
source: However, mysteries remain, with the most effective growth-inhibitory antibodies, 9AD4 and R5.016 not able to block basigin binding.
evidence: This is a statement in the introduction that sets up the research question.

claim: Basigin is a type I transmembrane protein of the immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily, with the most common isoform presenting an ectodomain consisting of two highly glycosylated extracellular Ig domains.
source: Basigin is a type I transmembrane protein of the immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily, with the most common isoform presenting an ectodomain consisting of two highly glycosylated extracellular Ig domains (Muramatsu, 2016), both of which contact PfRH5 (Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Muramatsu, 2016 and Wright et al., 2014.

claim: Both extracellular Ig domains of basigin contact PfRH5.
source: Basigin is a type I transmembrane protein of the immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily, with the most common isoform presenting an ectodomain consisting of two highly glycosylated extracellular Ig domains (Muramatsu, 2016), both of which contact PfRH5 (Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Wright et al., 2014.

claim: The transmembrane segment of basigin mediates formation of heteromeric complexes which contain basigin and either monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) or plasma membrane calcium ATPases (PMCAs).
source: More recently, the transmembrane segment of basigin has been shown to mediate formation of heteromeric complexes which contain basigin and either monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs) or plasma membrane calcium ATPases (PMCAs) (Muramatsu, 2016; Supper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Muramatsu, 2016 and Supper et al., 2016.

claim: MCTs are involved in proton-coupled exchange of lactate or pyruvate across plasma membranes.
source: MCTs are involved in proton-coupled exchange of lactate or pyruvate across plasma membranes (Felmlee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Felmlee et al., 2020.

claim: Both MCT1 and MCT4 interact with basigin in multiple eukaryotic cell lines.
source: Both MCT1 and MCT4 interact with basigin in multiple eukaryotic cell lines (Kirk et al., 2000), affecting their function and stability (Kirk et al., 2000) and MCT1 is the primary subtype in human erythrocytes (Juel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2000.

claim: MCT1 is the primary subtype in human erythrocytes.
source: Both MCT1 and MCT4 interact with basigin in multiple eukaryotic cell lines (Kirk et al., 2000), affecting their function and stability (Kirk et al., 2000) and MCT1 is the primary subtype in human erythrocytes (Juel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Juel et al., 2003.

claim: PMCAs play a role in membrane transport, with four subtypes of PMCA removing Ca2+ from the cell cytosol to maintain intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis and modulate cell signalling.
source: PMCAs also play a role in membrane transport, with four subtypes of PMCA removing Ca2+ from the cell cytosol to maintain intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis and modulate cell signalling (Stafford et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Stafford et al., 2017.

claim: Either basigin, or its close paralog neuroplastin, are essential subunits of PMCA, influencing expression and function of PMCAs in rodent neurons.
source: Either basigin, or its close paralog neuroplastin, are essential subunits of PMCA, influencing expression and function of PMCAs in rodent neurons, with human erythrocyte PMCAs complexed with basigin (Schmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2017.

claim: Human erythrocyte PMCAs are complexed with basigin.
source: Either basigin, or its close paralog neuroplastin, are essential subunits of PMCA, influencing expression and function of PMCAs in rodent neurons, with human erythrocyte PMCAs complexed with basigin (Schmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2017.

claim: Both basigin-MCT1 and neuroplastin-PMCA1 complexes have been structurally characterised, revealing interactions mediated by transmembrane helices.
source: Both basigin-MCT1 and neuroplastin-PMCA1 complexes have been structurally characterised, revealing interactions mediated by transmembrane helices (Gong et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), with the PfRH5 binding site on the basigin ectodomain remaining accessible.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2021.

claim: The PfRH5 binding site on the basigin ectodomain remains accessible in basigin-MCT1 and neuroplastin-PMCA1 complexes.
source: Both basigin-MCT1 and neuroplastin-PMCA1 complexes have been structurally characterised, revealing interactions mediated by transmembrane helices (Gong et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), with the PfRH5 binding site on the basigin ectodomain remaining accessible.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018 and Wang et al., 2021.

claim: PMCA1, PMCA4, and MCT1 are all expressed on human RBC plasma membrane.
source: Proteomics studies have confirmed that PMCA1, PMCA4, and MCT1 are all expressed on human RBC plasma membrane (Ravenhill et al., 2019) and, intriguingly, the actions of both MCTs and PMCAs have been linked to severe malaria (Bedu-Addo et al., 2013; Mariga et al., 2014; Timmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Ravenhill et al., 2019.

claim: The actions of both MCTs and PMCAs have been linked to severe malaria.
source: Proteomics studies have confirmed that PMCA1, PMCA4, and MCT1 are all expressed on human RBC plasma membrane (Ravenhill et al., 2019) and, intriguingly, the actions of both MCTs and PMCAs have been linked to severe malaria (Bedu-Addo et al., 2013; Mariga et al., 2014; Timmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Bedu-Addo et al., 2013; Mariga et al., 2014; Timmann et al., 2012.

claim: Cerebral malaria is associated with increased lactate concentrations, which may damage the blood-brain barrier.
source: In the case of MCT1, cerebral malaria is associated with increased lactate concentrations, which may damage the blood-brain barrier.
evidence: This is a statement in the introduction that provides context for the study.

claim: PMCA polymorphisms have been linked to the development of severe malaria in a genome-wide association study.
source: In contrast, PMCA polymorphisms have been linked to the development of severe malaria in a genome-wide association study, suggesting that calcium homeostasis across the erythrocyte membrane may affect the outcomes of malaria.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations in the introduction (Timmann et al., 2012).

claim: Spikes of increased intra-erythrocytic calcium have been observed during the parasite invasion process and these are dependent on the interaction between PfRH5 and basigin.
source: Spikes of increased intra-erythrocytic calcium have been observed during the parasite invasion process and these are dependent on the interaction between PfRH5 and basigin (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015), raising the question of whether localised blockage of PMCA-mediated calcium efflux may cause these calcium spikes.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Volz et al., 2016 and Weiss et al., 2015.

claim: Probing individual fractions with a basigin-binding antibody revealed a broad band indicating the presence of heterogeneously glycosylated basigin.
source: Probing individual fractions with a basigin-binding antibody revealed a broad band indicating the presence of heterogeneously glycosylated basigin.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Fractions rich in basigin also showed strong signals for both PMCAs and MCT1, indicating that the majority of basigin co-migrates with PMCAs and MCT1.
source: Fractions rich in basigin also showed strong signals for both PMCAs and MCT1, indicating that the majority of basigin co-migrates with PMCAs and MCT1 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The three components predominantly eluted in a region of the migration profile between standards of mass 157 kDa and 200 kDa, compatible with the mass of detergent-solubilised basigin-MCT1 and basigin-PMCA complexes.
source: The three components predominantly eluted in a region of the migration profile between standards of mass 157 kDa and 200 kDa, compatible with the mass of detergent-solubilised basigin-MCT1 and basigin-PMCA complexes (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: No basigin was found in later fractions in the region of the profile which would correspond to the mass of a single basigin in a detergent micelle.
source: No basigin was found in later fractions in the region of the profile which would correspond to the mass of a single basigin in a detergent micelle.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Insect cell expressed full-length basigin associates with binding partners in Sf9 cells which co-purify in DDM:CHS but are removed using the harsher detergent CHAPS.
source: We therefore concluded that insect cell expressed full-length basigin also associates with binding partners in Sf9 cells which co-purify in DDM:CHS but are removed using the harsher detergent CHAPS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: Full-length basigin purified in CHAPS and exchanged into DDM:CHS eluted at ~11.2 ml from a size exclusion column, later than the basigin-containing complexes extracted from erythrocytes.
source: This full-length basigin eluted at ~11.2 ml from a size exclusion column, later than the basigin-containing complexes extracted from erythrocytes (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The addition of the MCT1-specific antibody caused a shift in elution profile of the majority of the MCT1 and ~53% of basigin, suggesting them to be in complex.
source: While there was no shift of glycophorin C, the addition of the MCT1-specific antibody caused a shift in elution profile of the majority of the MCT1 and ~53% of basigin, suggesting them to be in complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ~47% of the basigin did not shift in the MCT1 antibody shift experiment.
source: However, ~47% of the basigin did not shift.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Western blotting 2D gels and staining with basigin, PMCA, and MCT1 antibodies indicated two separate populations of basigin-containing complexes, one of which co-migrated with PMCA and one of which co-migrated with MCT1.
source: Western blotting these 2D gels and staining with basigin, PMCA, and MCT1 antibodies indicated two separate populations of basigin-containing complexes, one of which co-migrated with PMCA and one of which co-migrated with MCT1.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Inclusion of an antibody which quantitatively binds to basigin shifted both populations to higher molecular weight.
source: Inclusion of an antibody which quantitatively binds to basigin shifted both populations to higher molecular weight (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Signals at the appropriate molecular weight for free basigin were not observed in either the presence or absence of the basigin-binding antibody.
source: Signals at the appropriate molecular weight for free basigin were not observed in either the presence or absence of the basigin-binding antibody (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), even upon prolonged exposure of the blots.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Sequential depletions of both PMCA and MCT1 resulted in almost complete elimination of basigin from the solubilised ghost membrane proteome.
source: Sequential depletions of both PMCA and MCT1 resulted in almost complete elimination of basigin from the solubilised ghost membrane proteome, confirming that nearly all basigin is complexed with one of these transporters.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Densitometric measurements showed ~72% of basigin complexed with MCT1 and ~28% of basigin complexed with PMCA.
source: Densitometric measurements also showed greater reduction in basigin levels upon MCT1 depletion, with ~72% of basigin complexed with MCT1 and ~28% of basigin complexed with PMCA.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed PMCA4 to be the major partner of basigin in human erythrocytes, while also identifying PMCA1.
source: This revealed PMCA4 to be the major partner of basigin in human erythrocytes, while also identifying PMCA1 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified MCT1 as the primary subtype of MCT in human erythrocytes, with MCT2 and -4 also detected.
source: Also identified were MCTs, with MCT1 as the primary subtype and MCT2 and -4 also detected (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The structure of the neuroplastin-PMCA1 complex shows the neuroplastin ectodomain to be presented above the extracellular loops of PMCA, with the surface of neuroplastin equivalent to that used by basigin to bind to PfRH5 being exposed.
source: The structure of the neuroplastin-PMCA1 complex shows the neuroplastin ectodomain to be presented above the extracellular loops of PMCA, with the surface of neuroplastin equivalent to that used by basigin to bind to PfRH5 being exposed, making it likely that PfRH5 can bind to PMCA-bound basigin (Figure 2a; Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2a and supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claim: It is likely that PfRH5 can bind to PMCA-bound basigin.
source: The structure of the neuroplastin-PMCA1 complex shows the neuroplastin ectodomain to be presented above the extracellular loops of PMCA, with the surface of neuroplastin equivalent to that used by basigin to bind to PfRH5 being exposed, making it likely that PfRH5 can bind to PMCA-bound basigin (Figure 2a; Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Basigin and PMCA eluted as a single peak on a size exclusion column, with an elution profile matching a 200 kDa standard, suggesting complex formation.
source: Basigin and PMCA eluted as a single peak on a size exclusion column, with an elution profile matching a 200 kDa standard, suggesting complex formation (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The purified basigin-PMCA complex showed Ca2+-dependent ATP hydrolysis activity.
source: The purified complex showed Ca2+-dependent ATP hydrolysis activity, confirming that active basigin-PMCA complexes had been isolated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Full-length basigin bound to PfRH5 with a dissociation constant of 0.56 µM.
source: Kinetic binding data for full-length basigin could be fitted to a 1:1 binding model with an affinity of 0.56 µM (χ2=2.44), in good agreement with the affinity of ~1 µM measured for basigin ectodomain in previous studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e; Crosnier et al., 2011; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The kinetic data for the basigin-PMCA complexes did not fit well to a 1:1 binding model but the fit improved significantly when using a two-state binding model.
source: In contrast, the kinetic data for the basigin-PMCA complexes did not fit well to a 1:1 binding model (χ2=7.71) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f), but the fit improved significantly (χ2=1.85) when using a two-state binding model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f, Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: PfRH5 bound to basigin-PMCA ~9-fold more tightly than to full-length basigin, primarily due to a lower dissociation rate constant.
source: PfRH5 therefore bound to basigin-PMCA ~9-fold more tightly than to full-length basigin, primarily due to a lower dissociation rate constant (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: The expression of PMCA4b and basigin, together with BKCa, in Chinese hamster ovary cells caused reduced intracellular Ca2+ concentrations, as demonstrated by a right shift in the BKCa activation curve.
source: The expression of PMCA4b and basigin, together with BKCa, in this system caused reduced intracellular Ca2+ concentrations, as demonstrated by a right shift in the BKCa activation curve.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Addition of PfRH5 at a concentration of 2 μM caused no change in the BKCa activation curve, indicating that PfRH5 binding did not modulate PMCA-basigin function and did not change the intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: We next added PfRH5 at a concentration of 2 μM which caused no further change in the BKCa activation curve, indicating that PfRH5 binding did not modulate PMCA-basigin function and did not change the intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Addition of PfRCR at a concentration of 1 μM caused no effect on intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: As PfRH5 is normally part of the three-component PfRCR complex, we also added PfRCR at a concentration of 1 μM to the same system. Here too, we observed no effect on intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and c.

claim: The extracellular peptide inhibitor caloxin 1c2 inhibited calcium-dependent ATP hydrolysis at high micromolar concentrations.
source: While the extracellular peptide inhibitor caloxin 1c2 inhibited calcium-dependent ATP hydrolysis at high micromolar concentrations, the addition of PfRH5 did not alter the ATPase activity of PMCA (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The addition of PfRH5 did not alter the ATPase activity of PMCA.
source: While the extracellular peptide inhibitor caloxin 1c2 inhibited calcium-dependent ATP hydrolysis at high micromolar concentrations, the addition of PfRH5 did not alter the ATPase activity of PMCA (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The PfRH5-binding site of basigin is exposed in the structure of the basigin-MCT1 complex.
source: As a large fraction of erythrocyte basigin is associated with MCT1, we also tested whether the basigin-MCT1 complex can bind to PfRH5, as the PfRH5-binding site of basigin is exposed in the structure of the basigin-MCT1 complex (Wang et al., 2021; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a statement based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3a and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Flowing solubilised ghost membrane extract over a chip surface coated with PfRH5 produced a binding response that reduced ~22% after depletion of PMCA-containing complexes.
source: Flowing solubilised ghost membrane extract over a chip surface coated with PfRH5 produced a binding response (Figure 3b). This reduced ~22% after depletion of PMCA-containing complexes, and the binding response was nearly absent for samples depleted for both PMCAs and MCT1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The binding response was nearly absent for samples depleted for both PMCAs and MCT1.
source: Flowing solubilised ghost membrane extract over a chip surface coated with PfRH5 produced a binding response (Figure 3b). This reduced ~22% after depletion of PMCA-containing complexes, and the binding response was nearly absent for samples depleted for both PMCAs and MCT1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Basigin in complex with either MCT1 or PMCAs can bind to PfRH5.
source: This suggests that basigin in complex with either MCT1 or PMCAs can bind to PfRH5.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The kinetic data for basigin-MCT1 binding to PfRH5 could be best described by a two-state binding model with a KD value of 93 nM.
source: Again, the kinetic data could be best described by a two-state binding model (χ2=3.09) with a KD value of 93 nM (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Longer periods of incubation of PfRH5 with the basigin-MCT1 complex lead to slower off-rates.
source: When we injected basigin-MCT1 over a chip decorated with biotinylated PfRH5, we indeed observed slower off-rates to be associated with longer incubation times, confirming a two-state interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Mixing basigin-MCT1 with PfRH5 for analysis by size exclusion chromatography showed formation of a stable complex.
source: We also mixed basigin-MCT1 with PfRH5 for analysis by size exclusion chromatography, and again observed formation of a stable complex (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: PfRH5 binds to both basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 with similar affinities, both more tightly than the interaction with the isolated basigin ectodomain.
source: Therefore, PfRH5 binds to both basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 with similar affinities, both more tightly than the interaction with the isolated basigin ectodomain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The basigin-targeting antibody, TRA-1–85, showed complete inhibition of P. falciparum growth at a 1 μg/ml concentration.
source: As previously shown, the basigin-targeting antibody, TRA-1–85, showed complete inhibition of growth at a 1 μg/ml concentration (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3e and supported by citation to Crosnier et al., 2011.

claim: Neither the PMCA or MCT1 antibodies caused growth inhibition at 75 μg/ml concentration.
source: However, neither the PMCA or MCT1 antibodies caused growth inhibition at 75 μg/ml concentration.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Only R5.004 prevented the binding of basigin ectodomain to PfRH5 immobilised on an SPR chip.
source: In accordance with previously published findings, only R5.004 prevented the binding of basigin ectodomain to PfRH5 immobilised on an SPR chip (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A similar outcome was seen for full-length basigin, showing that the presence of the detergent micelle is not sufficient to allow R5.016 to cause steric occlusion of binding.
source: A similar outcome was seen for full-length basigin, showing that the presence of the detergent micelle is not sufficient to allow R5.016 to cause steric occlusion of binding (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Both R5.016 and 9AD4 reduced binding of basigin-PMCA to immobilised PfRH5 by >90%.
source: In contrast, both R5.016 and 9AD4 reduced binding of basigin-PMCA to immobilised PfRH5 by >90% (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: R5.016 inhibited binding of basigin-PMCA to PfRH5 in a concentration-dependent manner, with concentrations of 100 nM or above producing nearly 90% inhibition.
source: Indeed R5.016 inhibited binding of basigin-PMCA to PfRH5 in a concentration-dependent manner, with concentrations of 100 nM or above producing nearly 90% inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Both R5.016 and 9AD4 reduced the binding of the basigin-MCT1 complex to immobilised PfRH5, with 100 nM of either antibody reducing binding by more than 50%.
source: Both R5.016 and 9AD4 also reduced the binding of the basigin-MCT1 complex to immobilised PfRH5, with 100 nM of either antibody reducing binding by more than 50% (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Neither of the non-inhibitory antibodies tested reduced the binding of basigin-PMCA or basigin-MCT1 to PfRH5.
source: In contrast, neither of the non-inhibitory antibodies tested reduced the binding of basigin-PMCA or basigin-MCT1 to PfRH5.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Binding of R5.016 and 9AD4 to PfRH5 would physically occlude its binding to basigin in the basigin-PMCA or basigin-MCT1 complexes, either through direct clashes with MCT1 or PMCA, or through a clash with the plasma membrane.
source: In both cases, binding of R5.016 and 9AD4 to PfRH5 would physically occlude its binding to basigin in the basigin-PMCA or basigin-MCT1 complexes, either through direct clashes with MCT1 or PMCA, or through a clash with the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural modeling shown in Figure 4d and 4e.

claim: Neutralising antibodies prevent PfRH5 from binding to basigin in the context of macromolecular basigin-containing complexes.
source: These data therefore support a model in which neutralising antibodies prevent PfRH5 from binding to basigin in the context of macromolecular basigin-containing complexes.

claim: No strain of P. falciparum has been identified which can take a basigin-independent invasion route.
source: To date, no strain of P. falciparum has been identified which can take a basigin-independent invasion route.
evidence: This is a statement in the discussion supported by prior knowledge.

claim: Vaccination or passive transfer of neutralising antibodies leads to protection of Aotus monkeys from parasite challenge.
source: Blocking this interaction also has proven therapeutic potential to prevent malaria, with antibodies against both PfRH5 and basigin identified which inhibit invasion (Alanine et al., 2019; Douglas et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014; Zenonos et al., 2015), with vaccination (Douglas et al., 2015) or passive transfer of neutralising antibodies (Douglas et al., 2019) leading to protection of Aotus monkeys from parasite challenge and with human vaccination slowing the onset of parasitaemia (Minassian et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Douglas et al., 2015 and Douglas et al., 2019.

claim: Human vaccination with PfRH5 slows the onset of parasitaemia.
source: Blocking this interaction also has proven therapeutic potential to prevent malaria, with antibodies against both PfRH5 and basigin identified which inhibit invasion (Alanine et al., 2019; Douglas et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014; Zenonos et al., 2015), with vaccination (Douglas et al., 2015) or passive transfer of neutralising antibodies (Douglas et al., 2019) leading to protection of Aotus monkeys from parasite challenge and with human vaccination slowing the onset of parasitaemia (Minassian et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to Minassian et al., 2021.

claim: Nearly all basigin in human erythrocyte membranes is found in complex with either PMCAs or MCTs.
source: To answer these questions, we started by investigating the immediate molecular context of basigin in human erythrocytes. Various studies in different cell types have shown that basigin forms heteromeric complexes with either PMCAs or MCTs (Muramatsu, 2016). We therefore used a combination of depletion, purification, 2D blue native PAGE, and mobility shift experiments to show that nearly all basigin in human erythrocyte membranes is found in complex with either PMCAs or MCTs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: While ~20% of basigin was not depleted with either PMCAs or MCT1, all basigin migrated at a high molecular weight on a size exclusion column.
source: While ~20% of basigin was not depleted with either PMCAs or MCT1 (Figure 1c), all basigin migrated at a high molecular weight on a size exclusion column and we did not observe free basigin in 2D blue native PAGE experiments.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The detection of free basigin in depletion experiments may be due to disruption of protein complexes during depletion experiments, or due to basigin in complex with subtypes or splice isoforms of PMCA or other subtypes of MCTs that are not efficiently depleted.
source: The detection of free basigin in depletion experiments may then be due to disruption of protein complexes during depletion experiments, or due to basigin in complex with subtypes or splice isoforms of PMCA or other subtypes of MCTs that are not efficiently depleted.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of experimental results.

claim: MCT1- and PMCA-bound basigin bind more tightly to PfRH5 than isolated full-length basigin.
source: Intriguingly, both MCT1- and PMCA-bound basigin bind more tightly to PfRH5 than to isolated full-length basigin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The binding of PfRH5 to basigin fits a simple 1:1 binding mode.
source: Indeed, fitting of kinetic binding data from SPR showed that, while the binding of PfRH5 to basigin fits a simple 1:1 binding mode, its binding to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 shows biphasic kinetics, which fit most closely to a two-state binding model.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The binding of PfRH5 to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 shows biphasic kinetics, which fit most closely to a two-state binding model.
source: Indeed, fitting of kinetic binding data from SPR showed that, while the binding of PfRH5 to basigin fits a simple 1:1 binding mode, its binding to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 shows biphasic kinetics, which fit most closely to a two-state binding model.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PfRH5 binds to basigin-MCT1 such that increasing association times correlate with decreasing dissociation rates.
source: This is further supported by data which shows that PfRH5 binds to basigin-MCT1 such that increasing association times correlate with decreasing dissociation rates, suggesting an initial lower affinity interaction, which 'matures' into a higher affinity interaction over time.
evidence: This is a description of experimental results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The two-state binding model is compatible with an initial lower affinity interaction between PfRH5 and basigin, followed by a subsequent interaction which stabilises the complex, possibly between PfRH5 and another part of the basigin-PMCA or basigin-MCT1 complexes.
source: While kinetic fitting data cannot be used to strictly derive a molecular mechanism, this is compatible with an initial lower affinity interaction between PfRH5 and basigin, followed by a subsequent interaction which stabilises the complex, possibly between PfRH5 and another part of the basigin-PMCA or basigin-MCT1 complexes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the molecular mechanism based on experimental data.

claim: PfRH5 is known to be essential for a spike of increased calcium concentration at the merozoite-erythrocyte junction.
source: However, PfRH5 is known to be essential for a spike of increased calcium concentration at the merozoite-erythrocyte junction (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015) and the presence of basigin has been shown to alter PMCA function (Schmidt et al., 2017).

claim: No change in basigin-PMCA function was observed in the presence of PfRH5 or of the PfRCR complex.

claim: Immunity to blood-stage malaria is antibody-mediated.
source: Immunity to blood-stage malaria is antibody-mediated and, while antibodies which target other aspects of the malaria life cycle use Fc-dependent mechanisms of immunity (Kurtovic et al., 2020; Teo et al., 2016), those which prevent invasion appear to function directly by blocking essential interactions (Alanine et al., 2019; Douglas et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claim: Antibodies which prevent invasion appear to function directly by blocking essential interactions.
source: Immunity to blood-stage malaria is antibody-mediated and, while antibodies which target other aspects of the malaria life cycle use Fc-dependent mechanisms of immunity (Kurtovic et al., 2020; Teo et al., 2016), those which prevent invasion appear to function directly by blocking essential interactions (Alanine et al., 2019; Douglas et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations to Alanine et al., 2019; Douglas et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2014.

source: As a result, the outcome of in vitro growth inhibition assays correlates well with protection due to PfRH5-targeting antibodies (Douglas et al., 2019).

claim: The most effective PfRH5-targeting neutralising antibodies from both humans (R5.016) and mice (9AD4) do not interfere with the PfRH5-basigin interaction.
source: It was therefore a mystery why the most effective PfRH5-targeting neutralising antibodies from both humans (R5.016) (Alanine et al., 2019) and mice (9AD4) (Douglas et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014) do not interfere with the PfRH5-basigin interaction.
evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claim: Both R5.016 and 9AD4 inhibit the binding of PfRH5 to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 complexes.
source: Studying basigin in the context of its membrane protein binding partners provides an answer, with both R5.016 and 9AD4 inhibiting the binding of PfRH5 to basigin-PMCA and basigin-MCT1 complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The inhibition by R5.016 and 9AD4 would be expected to be even stronger in the membrane context than in a detergent micelle.
source: While this inhibition is strong in the context of a detergent micelle, we would expect it to be even stronger in the membrane context, with both R5.016 and 9AD4 modelled to angle directly towards the membrane plane.
